newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan central bank says won't cool stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan central bank says won't cool stocks.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank governor on Thursday pledged not to intervene in the island's sizzling stock market, despite being "a bit worried" about red-hot share prices.

Sheu Yuan-dong said the sharp rise of the main stock index, which has soared more than 70 percent in the past year, was acceptable because its current level above 8,000 points is still far below an historic peak of more than 12,600 reached in 1990.
"The central bank is a bit worried about the recent stock market rally," Sheu told parliament in response to questions about central bank fiscal policy.
But he added: "The recent stock market rise shows that the market simply has returned to normal because it plunged too much in the past."
He was referring to a late 1990 tumble that dropped the market below 2,500.

The stock index gained 0.77 percent on Thursday to close at 8,081.00 points on frenzied turnover of T$174 billion (US$6.3 billion). The index has surged nearly 1,150 points, or 16.6 percent, in 1997 alone.

Some economists, including some of Sheu's central bank deputies, have voiced concern that the market's rise has been fuelled largely by an abundance of liquidity due to the bank's loose monetary policy and did not accurately reflect the value of Taiwan stocks.
But Sheu vowed to maintain a hands-off policy.
"The values of the shares should be determined by investors in the market," he said.

Sheu also pledged to refrain from commenting on the market after legislators scolded deputy central bank governor Hsu Chia-tung for warning on Saturday that investors should recognise the "danger" of a runaway market.
Hsu's comments caused a 1.29-percent plunge in the main index on Monday.
"We will make as little comment as possible on the stock market," Sheu said.

Analysts said Sheu's comments were in line with the government's policy of encouraging a strong bourse to boost the economy, which economists say is in the midst of a recovery, and to ensure healthy returns in the privatisation of state firms.
The Finance Ministry said in January that it planned to release some 800 million shares in state-owned firms worth T$100 billion (US$3.6 billion) in fiscal 1997/98 (July/June).
"Nobody can oppose the policy (of supporting a bullish stock market) now," said David Yu, vice-president at International Investment Trust Co.
Governor Sheu also reiterated the central bank's intention to lower banks' reserve requirements at the "appropriate" time, but gave no timetable.
"Taiwan's reserve requirements compared with other countries are a little bit too high," Sheu said. "The central bank will lower them at an appropriate time, but not now."

Sheu pledged to maintain the bank's longstanding "stable to loose" monetary policy, which aims to keep enough liquidity in circulation to ensure Taiwan's slowly accelerating recovery lasts without igniting inflation.
